  base $1/2$ and height greater than $4 A_*$, hence area greater than
  $A_*$. This triangle is contained in the convex hull of $p$ together
  with the worm vertices, so the hull's area exceeds $A_*$.

nodes.name: Grid polygonal worm
nodes.statement: Fix a step delta > 0 and a vertex count k in NN. A (k,delta)-grid polygonal worm is a pinned worm obtained by choosing grid points p_0, p_1, dots, p_k in deltaZZ times deltaZZ with p_0 = (0,0), setting tilde f(n/k) = p_n for 0 le n le k, and interpolating linearly on each interval [n/k, (n+1)/k], subject to the resulting curve being 1-Lipschitz.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:gridPolygonalWorm}
    
    
    Fix a step $\delta > 0$ and a vertex count $k \in \NN$. A
    \emph{$(k,\delta)$-grid polygonal worm} is a pinned worm obtained by
    choosing grid points $p_0, p_1, \dots, p_k \in \delta\ZZ \times \delta\ZZ$
    with $p_0 = (0,0)$, setting $\tilde f(n/k) = p_n$ for $0 \le n \le k$, and
    interpolating linearly on each interval $[n/k, (n+1)/k]$, subject to the
    resulting curve being $1$-Lipschitz.

nodes.name: The node bound is automatic
nodes.statement: Requiring in addition that the nodes p_0, dots, p_k lie within distance 1 of the origin does not change the set of (k,delta)-grid polygonal worms. Indeed the interpolant is 1-Lipschitz and pinned at the origin, so its whole range lies in the closed unit disc, and each node p_n with n le k is a value of it: p_n = tilde f(n/k).

nodes.name: The enumeration of grid worms is complete
nodes.statement: leanfileMoser/Real/NetEnumeration.lean Fix k ge 1 and c ge 1, and set delta = 1/(ck). A (k,delta)-grid polygonal worm is determined by integer node data: a sequence of k+1 pairs in ZZ^2 starting at (0,0) whose consecutive steps have squared Euclidean norm at most c^2. The executable branching enumeration netPaths — start at the origin and repeatedly branch over the finitely many admissible steps — is complete: every (k,delta)-grid polygonal worm is traced by a generated path.

nodes.name: Verified branch-and-bound $\varepsilon$-net
nodes.statement: leanfileMoser/Real/NetEnumeration.lean The enumeration is followed by a greedy bound. Since a convex cover contains a worm iff it contains the worm's convex hull, a path is redundant as soon as its hull is contained in an already-kept path's hull; the sweep hullPrunedNetPaths discards such paths, deciding hull coverage by an executable integer test (every node of the candidate lies in the hull of the keeper's nodes: point-on-segment by cross product and dot-product bounds, or point-in-triangle by common-sign cross products — complete in the plane by Carath\'eodory's theorem). For k ge 1 and c ge 2 the hulls of the surviving paths form an varepsilon-net of worms with the explicit tolerance varepsilon = 2/c + 1/k + 1/(ck); in particular for every varepsilon > 0, taking k = c ge max(2, 4/varepsilon) yields a finite, executably generated varepsilon-net. For c = 2 the bound shrinks the 13, 169, 2197 generated paths to 10, 65, 326 for k = 1, 2, 3.
conclusions: leanfileMoser/Real/NetEnumeration.lean The enumeration is followed by a greedy bound.

nodes.statement: Soundness of the point-in-triangle test: the three cross products are the barycentric numerators of the query point, and when they share a sign with the (nonzero) triangle determinant, dividing by the determinant exhibits the point as an explicit convex combination of the three vertices; point-on-segment handles the degenerate collinear cases, and hull-in-hull follows by testing every node. The greedy sweep maintains the invariant that every generated path is covered by some kept path (a dropped path by the keeper that witnessed dropping it; a kept path by itself). For the net property: by the quantitative form of the proof of Theorem~, every pinned worm lies within varepsilon of some (k,delta)-grid polygonal worm; by Theorem~ that worm is the polyline of a generated path; the polyline lies inside its own hull, that hull is contained in a kept path's hull, and thickenings are monotone under set inclusion. The elements of the net are convex sets rather than worms, which the definition of an varepsilon-net of worms permits.

nodes.name: The branch-and-bound worm search is sound
nodes.statement: leanfileMoser/Real/WormSearch.lean The branch-and-bound search of the blog post references only the tolerance varepsilon. A node consists of two point lists: points definitely in the worm's convex hull and points definitely not in it; the maybe region is implicit, so branching on a point x is a pure dichotomy (x is in the hull or it is not) and the search is exhaustive by construction. The search kills a branch when two included points are at distance > 1, or when the possible region lies in the varepsilon-thickening of a net element (for varepsilon ge 1, a net element within varepsilon - 1 of an included point suffices, since a worm hull has diameter at most 1; in general the box bigcap_A (A + [-1,1]^2) over included points is used); it adopts the included points into the net when they escape all varepsilon/2-thickenings; and both children of every branch are pruned by the redundancy rules: an included point in the hull of the other included points is dropped, and an excluded point D is dropped when another excluded point C lies in the hull of the included points together with D. If a fueled run closes every branch, the hulls of the collected net elements form an varepsilon-net of worms — unconditionally. For varepsilon ge 1 the run closes at the root with the singleton net \(0,0)\, checked at compile time; tolerances below 1 await a coverage test that exploits the excluded points (the region avoids the shadow cone of every excluded point, a union of 2^|excluded| convex pieces — the pruning is what keeps this exponent small). A strengthened length kill is specified but not yet implemented (IsStrongLengthKill): at slack varepsilon' it must pass every collection of included points containable in the hull of a length-1 worm and kill every collection not containable in a length-(1+varepsilon') worm; the gap between the thresholds is what makes the test finitely computable. Any conforming test slots into the search soundness unchanged (IsStrongLengthKill.no\_consistent), and the pairwise test satisfies the passing clause but not the killing clause (the vertices of a unit equilateral triangle are pairwise at distance 1 yet need a worm of length at least 3/2, by the half-perimeter lower bound). The kill side is implemented and verified (tourCertCheck, strongLengthKill): for any rational witnesses w_1, w_2, w_3 in the closed unit disc, probing with the directions d_j = w_j-1 - w_j forces one curve point beyond M(d_j) = max_p in I langle p, d_jrangle each; doubling the worm bounds the three-stop tour by 2L — with three stops the tour length is visit-order independent, so no permutation analysis is needed — while Cauchy--Schwarz and a cyclic rearrangement bound it below by sum_j M(d_j). Thus sum_j M(d_j) > 2, an exact rational check, kills soundly; witnesses along the edges of a spread triangle of included points recover the half-perimeter bound. The witness search is heuristic and carries no proof obligations. This strong kill is wired into the search. The passing clause also has a verified certificate (passCheck): a witness node list containing every included point whose k consecutive gaps are each at most (1+varepsilon')/k — exact rational checks — yields a (1+varepsilon')-Lipschitz piecewise-linear worm through the points (passCheck\_sound), with witnesses generated by greedy ordering and leg subdivision. What remains for a full IsStrongLengthKill instance is completeness: every collection is either killed by some tour certificate or passed by some witness.

The search kills a branch when two included points are at distance > 1, or when the possible region lies in the varepsilon-thickening of a net element (for varepsilon ge 1, a net element within varepsilon - 1 of an included point suffices, since a worm hull has diameter at most 1; in general the box bigcap_A (A + [-1,1]^2) over included points is used); it adopts the included points into the net when they escape all varepsilon/2-thickenings; and both children of every branch are pruned by the redundancy rules: an included point in the hull of the other included points is dropped, and an excluded point D is dropped when another excluded point C lies in the hull of the included points together with D.
If a fueled run closes every branch, the hulls of the collected net elements form an varepsilon-net of worms — unconditionally.

For varepsilon ge 1 the run closes at the root with the singleton net \(0,0)\, checked at compile time; tolerances below 1 await a coverage test that exploits the excluded points (the region avoids the shadow cone of every excluded point, a union of 2^|excluded| convex pieces — the pruning is what keeps this exponent small).

A strengthened length kill is specified but not yet implemented (IsStrongLengthKill): at slack varepsilon' it must pass every collection of included points containable in the hull of a length-1 worm and kill every collection not containable in a length-(1+varepsilon') worm; the gap between the thresholds is what makes the test finitely computable.

Any conforming test slots into the search soundness unchanged (IsStrongLengthKill.no\_consistent), and the pairwise test satisfies the passing clause but not the killing clause (the vertices of a unit equilateral triangle are pairwise at distance 1 yet need a worm of length at least 3/2, by the half-perimeter lower bound).

The kill side is implemented and verified (tourCertCheck, strongLengthKill): for any rational witnesses w_1, w_2, w_3 in the closed unit disc, probing with the directions d_j = w_j-1 - w_j forces one curve point beyond M(d_j) = max_p in I langle p, d_jrangle each; doubling the worm bounds the three-stop tour by 2L — with three stops the tour length is visit-order independent, so no permutation analysis is needed — while Cauchy--Schwarz and a cyclic rearrangement bound it below by sum_j M(d_j).
Thus sum_j M(d_j) > 2, an exact rational check, kills soundly; witnesses along the edges of a spread triangle of included points recover the half-perimeter bound.
The witness search is heuristic and carries no proof obligations.
This strong kill is wired into the search.

The passing clause also has a verified certificate (passCheck): a witness node list containing every included point whose k consecutive gaps are each at most (1+varepsilon')/k — exact rational checks — yields a (1+varepsilon')-Lipschitz piecewise-linear worm through the points (passCheck\_sound), with witnesses generated by greedy ordering and leg subdivision.
What remains for a full IsStrongLengthKill instance is completeness: every collection is either killed by some tour certificate or passed by some witness.

nodes.statement: Soundness of the kill rules: two points of a worm hull are at distance at most 1 (the worm has diameter at most 1; passing to hulls twice through closed balls transports the bound); the ball rule serves a worm by the triangle inequality through the included point; the box rule serves it because every vertex of the box is within varepsilon of the net hull (exact rational nearest-point computations) and thickenings of convex sets are convex. The redundancy principles are verified semantically: were a dropped excluded point D in the hull, convexity would force the witnessing excluded point C in as well. Pruning only removes constraints, so it weakens nodes and preserves consistency. The run soundness is an induction over the fuel: every pinned worm consistent with a stack node, or already served, is served by the final net; the net only grows; branching preserves consistency by the hull-membership dichotomy; and every pinned worm is consistent with the root (the origin is in its hull).

nodes.name: Moser cover number
nodes.statement: A set C subseteq RR^2 is a cover if for every worm f there is an orientation-preserving isometry (a translation--rotation) g of RR^2 such that the image of g circ f is contained in C. The Moser cover number M is the infimum of area(C) over all convex covers C.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:moserNumber}
    
    
    A set $C \subseteq \RR^2$ is a \emph{cover} if for every worm $f$ there is
    an orientation-preserving isometry (a translation--rotation) $g$ of $\RR^2$
    such that the image of $g \circ f$ is contained in $C$. The \emph{Moser
    cover number} $M$ is the infimum of $\area(C)$ over all convex covers $C$.

nodes.name: Minimal convex cover of a finite set of worms
nodes.statement: For a finite set S of worms, the minimal convex cover K(S) is a convex set of least area for which there exist translation--rotations (g_s)_s in S with the image of g_s circ s contained in K(S) for every s in S; that is, K(S) minimises area\!big(conv bigcup_s in S g_s(image\, s)big) over all choices of translation--rotations g_s.

\label{def:minimalCover}
    
    
    For a finite set $S$ of worms, the \emph{minimal convex cover} $K(S)$ is a
    convex set of least area for which there exist translation--rotations

nodes.statement: The minimal convex cover K(S) is the minimum, over all translation--rotations of the elements of S, of the area of the convex hull of their union. For a fixed finite S this is a finite-dimensional optimisation problem in the placement parameters and is in principle computable, e.g.\ by quantifier elimination over the reals, and plausibly by convex optimisation.
